newsitem.title: USA: Budget cuts could harm US scientific R&D - official.
newsitem.headline: Budget cuts could harm US scientific R&D - official.

text.p: Even modest budget cuts in federal spending for scientific research and development could cripple U.S. economic competitiveness in the future, a top Commerce Department official said Wednesday.
"You simply cannot afford to take this down below what we're doing now," Under Secretary for Technology Mary Good said at a meeting with reporters. "Anything less is suicidal."

In fiscal 1996, the United States spent about $71 billion for research and development. About $28 billion of that was spent on specific military projects with little or no spillover to civilian uses, Good said.

"If we don't spend this money today, our children and our grandchildren are not going to have access to the kinds of jobs in high-technology companies and all of the others we consider to be advantageous," Good said.

Military research and development spending and another $12 billion budgeted to the National Institutes of Health are unlikely to be cut, leaving the $31 billion spent on everything else vulnerable to severe cuts, Good warned.
That includes research on computers and the Internet, environmental technology, and energy and material products, Good said.

While U.S. spending remains level or is reduced, others continue to boost spending. Not including spending on military projects, Japan will outspend the United States in research and development next year for the first time, Good said.
"They are going to increase their R&D one more time in 1997," Good said. "This year, with an economy half our size, they will outspend us dollar for dollar," Good said.

To get more out of a limited budget, the Commerce Department is considering new initiatives combining public and private research efforts similiar to its electric car project. "We would very much like to do one in building and construction," Good said.
